english-definition:
finding. See FINDING OF FACT. finding of fact. (18c) A determination by a judge, jury, or administrative agency of a fact supported by the evidence in the record, usu. presented at the trial or hearing <he agreed with the jury's finding of fact that the driver did not stop before proceeding into the intersection>. comments: For our purposes, 'finding' and 'ruling' should be considered synonyms. See 'ruling' for more. Note that a 'finding' in English frequently is limited in scope; a judge or other fact finder may make a finding regarding a specific issue of fact or law, although it can be used more broadly ("I find you guilty" is technically a specific issue of law, but is often expressed using 'fallo' in Spanish). 'I've made a finding regarding removability', therefore, might more appropriately be a 'decisión', although 'the prebious IJ's finding regarding removability' could easily be 'el fallo del juez de lo migratorio previo en cuanto a la expulsabilidad' would also be appropriate.

[Cases: Courts C:";)88.] "A distinction is sometimes made between rules and rulings. Whether or not a formal distinction is declared, in common usage 'legal ruling' (or simply 'ruling') is a term ordinarily used to signify the outcome of applying a legal test when that outcome is one of relatively narrow impact. The immediate effect is to decide an issue in a single case. This meaning contrasts, for example, with the usual meaning of 'legal rule' (or simply 'rule'). The term 'rule' ordinarily refers to a legal proposition of general application. A 'ruling' may have force as precedent, but ordinarily it has that force because the conclusion it
expresses (for example, 'objection sustained') explicitly depends upon and implicitly reiterates a 'rule' a legal proposition of more general application ...." Robert E. Keeton, Judging 67-68 (1990). 2. Parliamentary law. The chair's decision on a point of order. rule, vb.

english-definition:
summary judgment. (18c) A judgment granted on a
claim or defense about which there is no genuine issue
ofmaterial fact and upon which the movant is entitled
to prevail as a matter oflaw .• The court considers the
contents of the pleadings, the motions, and additional
evidence adduced by the parties to determine whether
there is a genuine issue of material fact rather than
one of law. This procedural device allows the speedy
disposition ofa controversy without the need for trial.
Fed. R. Civ. P. 56. Also termed summary disposition;
judgment on the pleadings. See JUDGMENT.
comments: When an appeal is filed, opposing counsel generally files a motion for dismissal. This is, in many contexts, often referred to as a 'motion for summary judgment', and is often brought during trial, after a party has rested, as a way of pre-empting the remainder of the trial and asking the Judge to make a finding that said party has been unable to sustain their burden. A motion for summary dismissal is slightly different, in that it is made at the very beginning of a process (generally civil, administrative, or appellate), one could say before the process has already begun, and asks the appellate authorities to throw the case out due to legal or factual insufficiency. This is similar, but distinct in an important way, from a process that in Spanish is known as 'inadmisión a trámite'. In Spanish-language jurisdictions, commonly there is someone who has the authority (often a secretario judicial) and responsibility of deciding whether a case is admitted, or not, to the judicial process; this person makes a prima facie decision regarding jurisdiction and legal sufficiency, and either lo admite a trámite or lo inadmita a trámite. However, there is a fundamental difference here, because the person making the decision is the judicial authority itself, it is Court staff making a unilateral decision; a summary dismissal is action taken by the Court at the behest of counsel, already within the adversarial framework.

english-definition:
injunction (in-j3ngk-sh.m), n. (16c) A court order commanding or preventing an action. - To get an injunction, the complainant must show that there is no plain, adequate, and complete remedy at law and that an irreparable injury will result unless the relief is granted. - Also termed writ ofinjunction. See IRREPARABLE- INJURY RULE. [Cases: Injunction C;:::" 1.1 "In a general sense, every order of a court which commands or forbids is an injunction; but in its accepted legal sense, an injunction is ajudicial process or mandate operating in personam by which, upon certain established principles of equity, a party is required to do or refrain from doing a particular thing. An injunction has also been defined as a writ framed according to the circumstances of the case, commanding an act which the court regards as essential to justice, or restraining an act which it esteems contrary to equity and good conscience; as a remedial writ which courts issue for the purpose of enforcing their equity jurisdiction; and as a writ issuing by the order and under the
seal of a court of equity." 1 Howard C. Joyce. A Treatise on the Law Relating to Injunctions § 1, at 2-3 (1909).

english-definition: 1. To rule against; to reject <the judge overruled all of the defendant's objections>. 2. (Of a court) to overturn or set aside (a precedent) by expressly deciding that it should no longer be controlling law <in Brown v. Board ofEducation, the Supreme Court overruled Plessy v. Ferguson>. Cf. VACATE (1). [Cases: Courts (;=> 100(1).] "If a decision is not a recent one, and especially if it seems to be very poor, it should not be relied upon without ascertaining whether it may not have been expressly or impliedly overruled by some subsequent one; that is, whether the court may not have laid down a contrary principle in a later case." Frank Hall Childs, Where and How to Find the Law 94 (1922). "Overruling is an act of superior jurisdiction. A precedent overruled is definitely and formally deprived of all authority. It becomes null and void, like a repealed statute, and a new principle is authoritatively substituted for the old." John Salmond, Jurisprudence 189 (Glanville L. Williams ed., 10th ed. 1947).
